The idea that humans only use 10% of their brains is a common myth that has been debunked by experts in neuroscience and psychology. In reality, almost all areas of the brain are active almost all the time, and the brain is highly distributed and interconnected, meaning that different areas work together to perform various functions.

Brain imaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) have shown that even when we're not actively using a particular part of the brain, it's still active and performing background functions, such as regulating our body's automatic functions, like heart rate and breathing.

Additionally, studies of people with brain damage have shown that even small injuries to the brain can have significant effects on behavior and cognition, suggesting that almost all areas of the brain are important for our functioning.

So, while it's true that some areas of the brain may be more active at certain times than others, the idea that we only use 10% of our brains is an exaggeration and not supported by scientific evidence.
